item.title: Reverting a protected branch with git restore
item.description:
develop and main are usually protected: no reset, no force-push, so undoing anything means producing new commits on top. git revert does that, but it asks you to name a commit range, and every merge commit inside it needs a -m parent decision — on a branch with merges, that is a long list of chances to pick wrong.

git revert 4dbcaf5419d5b5aa19776d7ed733a163cacd95fe..dbffeb4da345fd0c66b0b7a8193a6582b409cd4a

The naive fallback is a second clone: check out the target branch in another folder, delete everything except .git, copy in the contents of the good branch, commit. It works and it is miserable.

item.title: Rebasing a messy branch in one conflict pass
item.description:
On a branch that has drifted behind a busy main, git rebase origin/main conflicts on the first commit and then asks for the same resolution again for each of the remaining ones — 16 conflicts instead of one. The trick is to stop rebasing commits you have already made and rebase an empty branch instead, then replay all the work as a single uncommitted change.

git checkout branch-to-rebase
git fetch --all
git merge-base branch-to-rebase origin/main # last commit before the branch's own work

Reset to that commit — every difference the branch introduced goes back to the working tree, unstaged:

item.title: Git aliases: scopes, shell escapes, and the ones I use
item.description:
Aliases are the difference between remembering git log --graph --oneline and typing git graph. They are ordinary config entries, so an alias only exists in the scope where it was created — and a command that needs a shell is still allowed.

Scope Applies to Config file
local the current repository .git/config (Windows: .git\config)
global the current user ~/.gitconfig (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.gitconfig)
system every user on the machine /etc/gitconfig (Windows: %PROGRAMDATA%\Git\config)

Creating one

git config --global alias.c "checkout"
git config --global alias.ec "commit --allow-empty -m 'Empty commit'" # single quotes when the command has double quotes

item.title: Git one-liners: prune, empty commits, show, grep, graph
item.description:
None of these are hidden features; they are the ones that quietly delete a step from a routine. Each one replaces four commands, a branch switch, or a commit you did not mean.

Prune on fetch

--prune deletes local references to remote branches that were themselves deleted:

git fetch --prune

Git keeps data unless told to throw it away, which extends to stale refs. Left to accumulate on a repo with branch churn, they make things like git branch -a --contains <commit> needlessly verbose and slow.
